text:
Apollo 13: The Long Way Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was making his fourth spaceflight and his second lunar voyage. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was to walk with him on the hills of Fra Mauro. Jack Swigert, the command module pilot, had joined the crew only days earlier, after Ken Mattingly was grounded for having been exposed to German measles. It was to be the third lunar landing, and the public had already begun to treat such flights as routine. The television networks did not carry the crew's broadcast live on the evening of April 13.

That broadcast ended with Lovell wishing viewers a good night. The spacecraft was about 200,000 miles from Earth, nearly 56 hours into the flight. It consisted of two vehicles docked nose to nose: the command module Odyssey, with its attached service module holding the main engine, oxygen and power supplies, and the spidery lunar module Aquarius, built only to land on the Moon and climb off it again.

A few minutes after the broadcast, Mission Control in Houston asked Swigert to perform a housekeeping task: switch on the fans that stirred the super-cold oxygen in the service module's tanks. He flipped the switches. Seconds later there was a loud bang, and the spacecraft shuddered. Warning lights came on across the instrument panel.

"Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here," Swigert radioed. Asked to repeat, Lovell said, "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first, controllers suspected faulty instruments, because the readings were too bad to be believed. One of the two oxygen tanks showed empty. The other was losing pressure. Two of the three fuel cells, which combined oxygen and hydrogen to make the ship's electricity and water, were dying. Then Lovell looked out the window and saw the truth for himself: the spacecraft was venting a cloud of gas into space. That gas was their oxygen, and with it went the command module's power, water and breathable air.

The Moon landing was lost within the hour. The question now was whether the crew could be brought home alive.

Flight director Gene Kranz and his team, and then the team led by Glynn Lunney that relieved them, came to the only available answer. Odyssey had to be shut down completely, to save its small reentry batteries and its last reserve of oxygen for the final hours of the flight, because it was the only vehicle with a heat shield. Until then, the crew would live in Aquarius. As the last fuel cell faded, Swigert powered down the command module while Lovell and Haise raced to bring the lunar module to life, transferring the guidance platform's alignment by hand, with Lovell checking his arithmetic against the controllers on the ground.

Aquarius had been designed to keep two men alive for about two days. It now had to sustain three men for about four. It had enough oxygen. Everything else was short.

The first decision was the route. Turning around directly would have required the main engine in the service module, and no one knew whether the explosion had damaged it. Instead, the crew would continue around the Moon and let its gravity sling them back. Using the lunar module's descent engine, which had never been intended for the job, they nudged their path onto a course that would return them to Earth. On the evening of April 14 they passed behind the Moon, farther from home than any humans before or since, and Swigert and Haise took photographs of the far side that Lovell knew he would never get to visit. Two hours after rounding the Moon, they fired the descent engine again for more than four minutes, cutting the trip home by about ten hours and aiming for a splashdown in the Pacific.

Then they began the long coast home. To save electricity, nearly everything in Aquarius was switched off, including the guidance computer and the heaters. The temperature in the cabin fell to a few degrees above freezing. Water condensed on the walls and instrument panels. The men slept badly, in snatches, in a cold that Lovell later compared to a damp cellar. Because water was needed to cool the lunar module's electronics, each man drank about six ounces a day, a fraction of what he needed. All three became dehydrated, and Haise developed a kidney infection and a fever.

A subtler danger was building in the air. Every breath the men exhaled added carbon dioxide to the cabin, and the lunar module's chemical scrubber canisters were being used up far faster than planned. The command module had plenty of spare canisters, but they were square, and the lunar module's sockets were round. In Houston, engineers piled on a table the things the crew had aboard, and worked out a way to join the two: plastic bags, the cardboard cover of a flight plan, a hose from a spacesuit, and gray duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew step by step. The contraption, which the astronauts called the mailbox, worked. The carbon dioxide level, which had been climbing toward dangerous levels, fell at once.

There was one more engine burn to make. Tracking showed the spacecraft drifting off course, shallow enough that it might miss the narrow corridor into the atmosphere. With the computer off, Lovell steered by eye, keeping the edge of Earth's shadow centered in his window while Haise held the ship steady in the other axis and Swigert timed the fourteen-second burn with his wristwatch.

Meanwhile, on the ground, Mattingly and a team of engineers led by John Aaron spent days in the simulators writing a procedure that had never existed: how to restart a frozen, dead command module on battery power so limited that the steps had to be done in exactly the right order. Swigert copied it down by hand over the radio. No one knew whether the soaked wiring behind Odyssey's panels would short out when the power returned. It did not.

On the morning of April 17, the crew cast off the service module and saw for the first time what had happened to it. "There's one whole side of that spacecraft missing," Lovell reported. An entire panel had been blown away, and wreckage hung out of the hole. Later they sealed themselves in Odyssey and released the lifeboat. "Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you," said the voice from Houston.

Reentry always brought a radio blackout of several minutes as hot gas enveloped the capsule. This one lasted almost a minute and a half longer than expected, while Mission Control waited in silence, unsure whether the heat shield had survived the explosion. Then Swigert's voice came through, and television screens showed three parachutes over the South Pacific. Odyssey splashed down near Samoa, a few miles from the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, almost six days after launch.

Investigators later traced the explosion to damaged wiring inside the oxygen tank, scorched during a ground test weeks before launch. It sparked when the fans were switched on. NASA called the flight a successful failure. The mission never reached the Moon, but all three of its crew came home.
